You don't need to create wrappers to `g_free`. That is, you can just pass `g_free` directly: `dlt->ecu_to_iface_ht = g_hash_table_new_full(g_int_hash, g_int_equal, g_free, g_free);`

Good point. It turns out that the code did not work as expected anyhow. :disappointed:

I cleaned up the error handling and removed the non-working robustness feature.

If keys are only just 32-bit, then there's no need for allocating them dynamically. Use `GINT_TO_POINTER()` and `GPOINTER_TO_INT()` to convert the key to/from pointer and pass `NULL` as key free function when constructing the hash table.

Same as with key. If the data is just 32-bit, then use `GUINT_TO_POINTER()` and `GPOINTER_TO_UINT()` instead and pass `NULL` as value free function when constructing the hash table.

changed this line in [version 9 of the diff](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/7453/diffs?diff_id=446970661&start_sha=a752570e4db1a5d947fbd96353fb058333f38fe9#e0c452992847449fb29fddb4fc7d94019504e4b5_118_99)

You can use `g_hash_table_lookup_extended()` to be able to determine between NULL and GUINT_TO_POINTER(0) if you decide to not dynamically allocate values.

Why `g_try_malloc0` instead of `g_malloc0`?

I assumed that we do not want Wireshark to crash on out of memory, so I used the same pattern as others (e.g. pcapng). However, I was not returning ENOMEM. This has been fixed now. So I assume your question is now resolved.

Well, header is so small that if we fail on it, things are going to be catastrophic.

However, the pattern to try alloc is when the allocation size is coming from tainted source, e.g. from the capture file itself. In such case we don't want to abort on out of memory as it can simply be malicious file.

Fine for me too. I changed the first one to g_malloc0, since it has a fixed length that is quite small. The second instance I left as g_try_malloc0, since the length is based on the header the code reads from the file.

@guyharris Any reason why this is not being accepted?

Unfortunately, "DLT" is used in libpcap for "data link type", with "a DLT" being used for a link-layer type code.

Using "AUTOSAR Diagnostic Log and Trace" in long descriptions, "AUTOSAR Dlt" (capitalization as per the spec) in shorter text, and "autosar-dlt" or something such as that in file names, etc. might help distinguish between them.

@guyharris Which parts are you referring to? All the wiretap code? (mime_type.c, file_access.c, dlt.c, ...) ? Also file-dlt.c as well? I would prefer not the change the dissector (packet-dlt.c) since this is present like this since a long time and should not change the name because of this.

AUTOSAR specifies a software module to implement the protocol and calls it sometimes Dlt or DLT (being the module). Since this is basically the best specification publicly available right now, this is what I referenced. Commonly the protocol itself is called DLT. But I think capitalization is not the issue.
